findings.explanation:
Construction delegates to a private constructor with concurrency level 16. It rejects negative capacities through `Assert.isTrue(capacity >= 0, ...)` (an `IllegalArgumentException`), accepts zero, and creates a `ConcurrentHashMap` with initial capacity 16, load factor 0.75, and concurrency-level hint 16. That hint configures the backing map; it is not a limit on generator concurrency.

At capacity zero, every `get` directly invokes the generator and bypasses the map, queues, and positive-capacity null check. Consequently, even a null result is returned and never cached. For positive capacity, a map hit records a read and returns the node's retained value. A miss invokes the generator before any eviction lock is involved, passes the result to `put`, and returns that caller's local generated value.

Generation is not single-flight or serialized per key. Competing miss callers may generate concurrently. At `putIfAbsent`, one node wins and receives an `AddTask`; a loser records a read against the returned `prior` node—the winning cached node, not its discarded candidate. Each caller nevertheless returns its own generated value, so a loser can return a value different from the one installed in the cache. If the mapping disappears before a contender's `putIfAbsent`, that contender can instead become an inserter.

For positive capacity, `Assert.notNull(value, ...)` runs before `putIfAbsent`, so a generated null throws `IllegalArgumentException` even if another miss has meanwhile installed a value. Generator exceptions are not caught in either the zero-capacity or ordinary miss path; they propagate, and this call performs no insertion handoff.

Both ordinary cache hits and `putIfAbsent` losers call `processRead`. Recording chooses one of four buffers from the current thread ID's low two bits. Each buffer is a bounded 128-slot ring: `MAX_PENDING_OPERATIONS` is 32, `MAX_DRAIN_COUNT` is 64, and buffer size is 128. Threads are striped rather than given exclusive buffers, so different threads can select the same buffer.

`recordRead` advances that buffer's recorded count with lazy stores and writes the node into the corresponding ring slot. Using the pre-increment count, recorded-minus-processed below 32 is considered delayable; once the old pending count is at least 32, an IDLE cache attempts a drain. Recording itself does not move the node in the LRU queue.

A read drain visits all four buffers once, in a rotated order beginning with a buffer derived from the draining thread ID. For each buffer, this helper snapshots `recordedCount`, consumes at most 64 slots, and stops earlier at the first null. Each consumed slot is cleared, its node is offered to `moveToBack`, and `readCount` advances. At the end, `processedCount` is set to the earlier recorded-count snapshot even if a null or the 64-item limit stopped consumption; it is therefore a scheduling estimate rather than a count of loop iterations.

`moveToBack` moves a node only if it is currently linked in the eviction queue and is not already the tail. A not-yet-added, unlinked/removed, or already-last node is ignored; the helper does not separately inspect entry state. Actual queue changes are serialized by the eviction lock, but reads are recorded concurrently and later drained in per-buffer batches without merging the buffers by global access time. Lazy striped recording, possible same-buffer collisions or ring reuse, delayed draining, and bounded consumption therefore do not promise one synchronous, globally ordered LRU update for every read.

A write first enters a `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`, publishes status REQUIRED, and asks the same caller to drain. There is no executor or background maintenance thread: gets, insert handoffs, and removals opportunistically perform maintenance themselves.

For reads, IDLE attempts draining only when the recorded read is no longer delayable; REQUIRED always attempts because a write is pending; PROCESSING suppresses a nested read-driven attempt. `drainOperations` uses nonblocking `tryLock`. Failure simply leaves buffered work for the lock holder or a later caller. In particular, a write normally leaves REQUIRED published when its attempt loses the lock, while an IDLE read trigger does not create a separate maintenance job.

After acquiring the lock, a caller publishes PROCESSING, drains reads before writes, and normally executes at most 16 queued write tasks (`WriteOperations.DRAIN_THRESHOLD`). Work beyond that bound can remain queued for a subsequent drain. The `finally` block resets PROCESSING to IDLE only with a CAS and always unlocks. If another writer publishes REQUIRED while draining is in progress, the CAS fails and preserves REQUIRED for a future attempt.

The eviction lock serializes queue reordering, maintenance accounting, eviction, and clear operations. It does not wrap generator execution, ordinary concurrent-map lookup/insertion/removal, or every read recording operation.

A winning `putIfAbsent` changes the backing map immediately and only afterward enqueues the `AddTask`; the winning caller may execute it inline if it acquires the drain lock, but that is not guaranteed. A new node starts ACTIVE.

When eventually run under the eviction lock, `AddTask` increments internal `currentSize` unconditionally, even if removal has already made the node inactive. That unconditional increment allows separately queued removal accounting to balance insertion regardless of task ordering. Only an ACTIVE node is linked at the queue tail and invokes capacity enforcement.

While internal accounting exceeds capacity, eviction polls the queue front—the oldest entry according to the presently drained LRU order. An empty queue terminates enforcement even if accounting is still over capacity, which can occur while inactive or not-yet-linked work is pending. Removal from the map is identity-conditional (`remove(key, node)`), so an old queued node cannot delete a newer replacement with the same key. The polled node is then marked removed regardless of whether that conditional map removal succeeded.

`markAsRemoved` repeatedly snapshots the node and CASes in a new entry containing the same value and REMOVED state, then lazy-decrements `currentSize`. It has no active-state predicate, so the decrement is per successful helper invocation rather than intrinsically guarded as an exactly-once transition.

`currentSize` is private maintenance accounting; public `size()` reads `cache.size()`. Map insertion precedes accounting, map removal can precede cleanup, normal drains process only 16 writes, and read recency is buffered. Thus the public map can temporarily—and without another maintenance-triggering caller, potentially persistently—exceed capacity, while eviction order reflects drained rather than instantaneously globally ordered accesses. Capacity enforcement and queue mutation are serialized under one lock, but they are not atomic with concurrent map changes.

`remove` first performs the backing map's immediate atomic removal. No mapping returns false and schedules nothing; successfully removing a node returns true after scheduling its maintenance. Another insertion can of course make the key present again independently.

For a removed mapping, `markForRemoval` preserves the value while CASing ACTIVE to PENDING_REMOVAL. It retries after a failed CAS and exits without changing an already-pending or REMOVED node. A `RemovalTask` is then queued regardless of whether the helper found the node already inactive. When that task runs under the eviction lock, it unlinks the node if still present in the eviction queue and invokes `markAsRemoved`, which retains the value, installs REMOVED, and performs the internal accounting decrement. The caller may drain this task before returning, but lock contention or the normal write-drain limit can defer it.

Accordingly, key visibility and public map size change before queue membership and `currentSize` necessarily do. Removal also does not cancel a `get` that obtained the old node before the map removal: that retrieval can still record the detached node and return its retained value; a later recency drain simply ignores it once it is no longer linked.

Unlike opportunistic maintenance, `clear` takes the eviction lock with blocking `lock()` and releases it in `finally`. It polls every node currently in the LRU queue, identity-conditionally removes that node from the backing map, and marks it REMOVED with accounting cleanup. It then nulls every read-buffer slot using lazy stores; it does not reset `recordedCount`, `readCount`, or `processedCount`. Finally, it drains queued write tasks with no 16-task bound, continuing until the concurrent write queue is observed empty.

The method never calls `cache.clear()`, and it does not poll the eviction queue again after `drainAll`. A queued `AddTask` processed during that final phase can therefore account and link an ACTIVE mapping that remains after clear. Likewise, concurrent insertion can change the map while clear holds the maintenance lock, including the window between `putIfAbsent` and AddTask enqueue. Identity-conditional removal also intentionally preserves a newer replacement. Thus clear serializes queue/accounting maintenance and blocks other clear/drain holders, but it does not stop generation or ordinary concurrent-map operations and cannot promise an unconditional atomic-empty instant in their presence.

`size()` observes the backing `ConcurrentHashMap.size()`, not `currentSize`; `contains(key)` observes `containsKey` and neither generates nor records recency. `capacity()` returns the immutable configured capacity, and deprecated `sizeLimit()` is the same value.

`src/test/java/org/springframework/util/ConcurrentLruCacheTests.java` lines 34-108 corroborate quiescent sequential behavior: zero capacity generates without storing, three inserts into capacity two evict the oldest, explicit removal updates public observations, and clear empties the two inserted entries. Those single-threaded tests contain no competing operations or delayed-maintenance orchestration, so they are not evidence of atomic clearing, strict concurrent capacity, or globally ordered concurrent LRU behavior.
